acquisition.why: The source plan relies on permissionless DMs to local businesses. Most UK restaurants and trades are sole traders or partnerships, so PECR bans that. Legal routes are Meta ads showing a sample video, and cold email to Ltd companies and estate-agency firms. Both need a human to judge targeting and the pitch.

onboarding.why: An intake form plus brand assets and photos can be agent-collected. Some back-and-forth on tone and claims is still needed.

delivery.why: Veo or Sora prompt pipelines per niche can generate the videos. A human must QA output for the AI look, for misleading 'fake testimonial' content (CPRs and CAP), and for property misrepresentation (material information rules).

support.why: Revision requests, churn when ads don't perform, and taste disputes. These are human-heavy for a retainer creative service.

scores.R_why: Cheap to test (a Veo subscription costs about £100 [E]). But 6-8 h/week covers little beyond revisions, and the restaurant or trade buyer is often a sole trader reachable only in person. Fake-review-style AI videos breach the DMCC Act 2024 fake review rules and the CAP Code. No first-hand evidence that anyone has bought.
scores.M_why: Very crowded in 2026. Every agency and freelancer sells AI reels, and the owners themselves can use CapCut, Veo and platform-native AI ad tools. Listing-to-video is built into portals and CRM tools [E]. Price is collapsing.
scores.one_line: Hypothetical, rapidly commoditised AI-reel retainer. Legal UK acquisition is hard and the creative QA and revisions need a human, so it is a poor fit for an agent-run business.

acquisition.why: Several inbound routes are legal: an SEO page per niche ('UK beauty micro-influencers'), an Apify Store actor, or a Gumroad/Etsy-style data product. Cold email to brand limited companies is also fine. Discovery depends on the platforms.

onboarding.why: Self-serve criteria form, or a subscription to filtered lists.

delivery.why: Apify scrapers plus LLM enrichment can run unattended. Scrapers break, and data quality needs spot-checks.

support.why: Data accuracy complaints and refunds, partly handled by agents.

scores.R_why: Technically easy for Ricardo and close to £0 to test. However, compiling and selling creators' personal contact data is processing under UK GDPR. It needs a legitimate interests assessment, Art. 14 transparency and the ICO fee. It also breaches the platforms' terms (Instagram, TikTok). A $10/mo price means you need many customers.
scores.M_why: Saturated by Modash, Upfluence, HypeAuditor, Heepsy, and TikTok/IG creator marketplaces with official APIs. LLM agents (Lindy demo) let brands do this themselves. Platform anti-scraping risk is high.
scores.one_line: Highly automatable, but it is a GDPR and terms-of-service-risky data play competing with well-funded SaaS and free official creator marketplaces. There is little room for a solo UK entrant.

acquisition.why: Inbound only: SEO pages ('digital waiver for Scout groups', 'paddleboard hire waiver UK'), Meta ads and community posts. Paid ads proved uneconomic at a $13/yr price, so it relies on slow SEO plus referral links in the emails signers receive.

onboarding.why: Self-serve event creation and a shareable link, with no account needed for signers.

support.why: Agents can answer how-to questions. Questions about whether a waiver is enforceable must get a templated 'not legal advice' answer, and bugs need Ricardo.

scores.R_why: A good skills match: Ricardo can build it in a few weekends and hosting costs under £300. The burden is children's medical (special category) data, which needs a DPIA, a security posture, ICO registration and hosting in the UK or EU. UK liability waivers are also weaker: under UCTA you cannot exclude liability for negligent death or injury, so the value is mostly consent, medical info and check-in rather than a 'waiver'. Only one first-hand customer is reported.
scores.M_why: Incumbents include Smartwaiver, WaiverForever, WaiverSign and the waiver features in booking tools (Bookwhen, FareHarbor, Rezdy). Real gaps remain in cheap consent forms for UK clubs and youth groups (Scouts, churches, sports clubs) [E], but willingness to pay is low and seasonal.
scores.one_line: A genuinely agent-runnable micro-SaaS with low build cost. The UK angle should be 'consent and medical forms' for clubs and hire shops. Low prices and incumbents limit the upside, and child data compliance is the main burden.

acquisition.why: Inbound and legal: Beehiiv recommendations and boosts, SEO, and organic posts on X and Reddit. Growth is slow and depends on the platforms.

delivery.why: Agents can draft the news digest. The money is in events and group trips, which are physical, human-run, and carry package-travel and ATOL obligations.

support.why: Newsletter support is easy. Event and trip support is human.

scores.R_why: One untested hypothetical. Ricardo cannot run tours or conferences with a toddler and 6-8 h/week. Package Travel Regulations need insolvency protection. Band trademark issues arise if it looks official. The newsletter alone monetises poorly.
scores.M_why: Fan niches are plentiful but small. Official fan clubs, Reddit, Discord and artist-run Patreon communities already serve superfans. AI-written music news is commoditised.
scores.one_line: An agent can write the newsletter, but the revenue sits in physical, regulated events and trips, from a single speculative mention. It is unsuitable.

acquisition.why: The best channels in the source are in-person networking and cold calls, which need a human. Cold texting is illegal to UK sole traders. Legal and agent-runnable: an agent finds Ltd companies using old chat widgets via BuiltWith, auto-builds a demo bot and cold-emails it. Shopify App Store or agency-partner listings also work.

onboarding.why: Scraping the site and docs into a bot is automated. Access, escalation rules and tone need a human call.

delivery.why: Platforms such as DocsBot run the bot. AI-generated monthly reports and knowledge-gap fixes are mostly agent work.

billing.why: Stripe setup fee plus retainer. Larger clients may need invoices.

support.why: Wrong answers or refund mishaps create escalations that need a human, plus GDPR processor terms (a DPA).

scores.R_why: Ricardo has the technical skill, and the test is cheap (DocsBot, Apollo and a domain, about £100 [E]). Selling £1.5k setup fees still usually needs calls. Liability for wrong answers and UK GDPR processor duties apply. It is feasible at small scale.
scores.M_why: Heavily saturated in 2026. Intercom Fin, Zendesk AI, Tidio, Gorgias and Shopify Inbox AI are built in or cheap self-serve. Thousands of 'AI automation agencies' cold-email the same prospects. Retainer value is eroding as SMBs switch it on themselves.
scores.one_line: Well-trodden and automatable, with legal B2B cold email. But commoditisation by native helpdesk AI and a sea of agencies make durable £500/mo retainers unlikely.

acquisition.why: Inbound: SEO for 'buy X online UK', a press pitch (cold email to journalists at media companies is fine), organic virality and an email list. It depends on a novelty hook.

delivery.why: Buying at full retail in physical stores, transporting, warehousing, and picking, packing and shipping food and merch.

support.why: Order queries can be handled by agents. Damaged food and returns need a human.

scores.R_why: Physical sourcing trips and fulfilment don't fit 6-8 h/week with a toddler. £300 of stock is tiny. UK food resale needs council food business registration and labelling (allergens), and branded resale carries trademark risk. A UK cult brand with no online store is hard to find [E]; most already sell online.
scores.M_why: Depends on a brand with unmet online demand, which can vanish the moment the brand launches e-commerce or objects. Thin margins at full retail. Proven in the US only.
scores.one_line: Well-corroborated (4 first-hand videos) real business. But it is physical sourcing and fulfilment with brand-dependency risk, so it is close to the opposite of an agent-run UK side business.

acquisition.why: Consumer-side leads come inbound via paid search and social, which is legal. Selling to buyers needs consent-backed data transfer under PECR and UK GDPR. Recruiting buyer businesses (many are sole-trader cleaners and roofers) is often not legal by cold DM or SMS, so needs calls, ads or Ltd-company email.

onboarding.why: Buyer agreements on price, exclusivity and refunds need negotiation. Lead routing can then be automated.

delivery.why: Landing pages, forms and routing via Zapier or a CRM are automatable. Ad optimisation is semi-automated but budget-sensitive.

billing.why: Per-lead invoicing and disputes over lead quality and credits.

support.why: Buyers dispute lead quality and consumers complain. Human judgement is needed.

scores.R_why: £300 barely buys a couple of weeks of UK Google Ads in competitive trades (cleaning or roofing CPCs of about £3-10 [E]). Consent wording for passing leads on, plus UK GDPR controller duties, are required. Claims, solar finance and insurance verticals are FCA-regulated: avoid them. Testing a niche B2B vertical (e.g. aggregates or skips) is possible.
scores.M_why: Competes with Checkatrade, MyBuilder, Bark and Google Local Services Ads. Rising CPCs squeeze arbitrage. Obscure B2B or materials niches have some room.
scores.one_line: Automatable machinery, but the hypothetical economics are thin at £300 of ad budget. UK consent and regulation rules plus Bark-style incumbents make it marginal; only obscure niches look viable.

acquisition.why: Inbound: content, SEO, YouTube, newsletter cross-promotion and Skool discovery. All examples rely on the founder's existing audience, which Ricardo lacks.

onboarding.why: Platform signup and automated welcome flows.

delivery.why: A community needs authentic founder presence and moderation. Agents can seed prompts, digests and events, but members detect inauthenticity.

support.why: Agents handle access and billing questions. Moderation disputes need a human.

scores.R_why: Low cost, but it requires Ricardo to be a credible insider of a niche and to grow an audience from zero within 6-8 h/week. The first-hand case shows only $5/mo × ~210 members. The other examples are untested.
scores.M_why: Skool, Circle and Discord communities are abundant, and churn is high. Niches are endless but monetisation needs authority. AI chat substitutes some of the 'learning' value but not the human connection.
scores.one_line: Inbound and billing are automatable, but value depends on a human founder's identity and an audience Ricardo doesn't have. It only fits if he picks a niche he already lives in.
